one_liner: Hardware proposal: a small in-order support core runs malloc/free for all cores; simulated 1.15x over mimalloc and 1.75x over jemalloc at 16 threads.
what_it_does: SpeedMalloc (Ruihao Li, Lizy K. John et al., UT Austin; arXiv 2508.20253, also listed as an IEEE CAL 2025 paper) moves memory allocation off the application cores onto a dedicated microcontroller-grade programmable core that takes about 1-2% of chip area. Application threads send malloc() and free() requests to it through four new ISA instructions (mallocstart, freestart, mallocend, freeend) plus signal and data packets, inserted by a modified compiler. It is an architecture proposal evaluated in simulation, not a software library.
how_it_is_fast: All allocator metadata lives in the support core's own L1 caches (for example a 16 KB L1-D), so it no longer pollutes the main cores' L1/L2 and evicts user data. Because one core serializes every metadata update, the allocator needs no atomics and no cross-core metadata synchronization. Hardware message queues with a dispatch queue, a priority scheduler and round-robin fairness absorb bursts; the invocation path is assumed to take 8 cycles.
when_to_use: Architecture research on allocator offload, metadata cache pollution or heterogeneous helper cores
Citing a simulated upper bound for what removing allocator synchronization could buy multi-threaded, allocation-heavy code
Comparing against hardware allocator accelerators such as Mallacc and Memento
when_not_to_use: Any real software project: no existing CPU has the support core or the ISA extensions
As evidence that mimalloc or jemalloc can be beaten on current hardware: every number comes from gem5 simulation
When you need reproducible numbers: no code, gem5 configuration or modified compiler release was found
Single-threaded programs: the claimed benefit comes from removing cross-core synchronization

integration.form: not applicable (hardware/ISA proposal; no software artifact released)
integration.dependencies: custom hardware support core, ISA extensions and compiler changes
integration.platforms: simulated AArch64 only (gem5 full system, McPAT for power and area)
integration.thread_safety: Serializes all allocator metadata updates on the single support core

gotchas: The 1.75x/1.18x/1.15x figures are for 16-thread workloads, not an average over thread counts
Energy and area figures come from McPAT models, not silicon
One support core serves all main cores; the paper says it is not a bottleneck at the core counts simulated, but scaling beyond them is not documented here
The 8-cycle invocation latency is an assumption of the model
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Never as a library. Every sibling (v8malloc, Mesh, LLFree, fast-alloc) runs on today's CPUs; cite SpeedMalloc only when the question is hardware offload. Exgen-Malloc, from the same group, is the software single-thread counterpart.
verified_claims_summary: In full-system gem5 simulation of AArch64 cores (with McPAT power/area modelling), the paper reports 16-thread speedups of 1.75x over jemalloc, 1.18x over TCMalloc, 1.15x over mimalloc, 1.23x over Mallacc and 1.18x over Memento+, with equal or lower energy; allocator versions, workloads and core configuration could not be checked because the paper was blocked and only search snippets were read.
status_note: Simulation-only research proposal with no code release; reference only and not usable on existing hardware.
